text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Internal unrest continues inside Denmark's opposition Conservative Party with calls by the new leader Per Stig Moeller for discipline. Moeller was elected party leader when his predecessor Hans Engell resigned s after being involved in a car accident and found to have a higher than legal blood alcohol level. Moeller himself, it later transpire, tried to hush up a drunken-driving offence he committed as a student.
--The opposition left-wing Socialist People's Party has rejected proposals from the ruling Social Democrats to enter a political alliance up to November's local elections in Denmark.

--Price-conscious Danish private borrowers are switching from orthodox banks to discount banks and mortgage credit institutions, with Danske Kredit and Unikredit, owned by the two biggest banks Den Danske Bank and Unidanmark showing the greatest growth. So-called flex loans at mortgage credit firm Realkredit Danmark are also doing well.

--There is optimism about the prospects of a completion before Easter of negotiations on a 48 percent takeover of troubled J. Lauritzen shipyard Danyard by Malaysian financier Amin Shah. Transfer of the necessary funds to Denmark has to be approved by the Malaysian authorities.

--According to a survey, 41 percent of Danish industrial chiefs expect increasing sales, more orders and bigger profits both in domestic and export markets in the next six months, with only six percent predicting falls. This gives rise to hopes that unemploymenmt can be brought below 200,000 in Denmark without causing any marked increase in inflation.
